title: Interpreting building automation system alerts on Mac: a guide for facilities managers
metaTitle: Interpreting building automation system alerts: a guide for facilities managers
description: Learn how to manage alert fatigue and prioritize building automation system alerts on your Mac to reduce downtime and improve operational efficiency.
intro: Interpreting building automation system alerts requires a clear strategy to filter noise from critical equipment failures. You can manage this volume on your Mac by centralizing your data and applying risk-based scoring to your daily notifications.
tldr: Alert fatigue occurs when too many low-priority notifications cause you to miss critical system failures.
Use intelligent scoring to rank alerts by asset criticality rather than just time of arrival.

blocks.text: The challenge of interpreting building automation system alerts

Facilities managers face a constant barrage of data. Your building automation system, or BMS, is designed to keep you informed. However, it often notifies you for every minor event. A door held open for a delivery triggers the same urgency as a cooling system failure. This creates a state of alert fatigue. You become desensitized to the constant pinging of your inbox or dashboard. When every event looks urgent, you eventually stop treating any of them as critical.
Why alert fatigue happens in your facility

The primary cause is a lack of context. Your system knows an event happened, but it does not know if that asset is currently critical to your operations. It does not look at the age of the equipment or the service history. You end up with fragmented systems. You might have a spreadsheet for maintenance schedules, an email inbox for vendor requests, and a separate portal for BMS alerts. These tools do not talk to each other. You spend your morning manually consolidating this information on your Mac just to see what needs attention first.
How to fix alert prioritization without new software

items: Audit your current alarm thresholds. Ask your controls contractor to disable non-critical alerts that do not require an immediate site visit.
Create a simple priority matrix. Define what constitutes a P1 emergency versus a P3 routine maintenance task.
Set up email rules in Apple Mail. Use the Mail > Rules menu to move specific alert types into dedicated folders so your main inbox stays clear for urgent vendor communication.
Schedule a daily review session. Spend 15 minutes each morning looking at the previous day's alert logs to identify patterns or recurring nuisance alarms.

blocks.text: If you are in a regulated environment, ensure your alert handling procedures align with your company's safety and data compliance policies.

blocks.text: Using Lazur to manage your daily alerts

Lazur helps you cut through the noise by acting as an assistant on your Mac. When you have a screen full of alerts or a long list of emails from your BMS, you can use Lazur to summarize the situation. Instead of reading every single notification, hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask Lazur to identify the most critical items. It can point you to the specific work order or email thread that needs your attention first.

faq.question: What is alert fatigue in facilities management?
faq.answer: Alert fatigue is a condition where facilities managers become desensitized to constant system notifications because of the high volume of non-critical or false alarms, leading to delayed responses for actual emergencies.

faq.question: How can I reduce the number of BMS alerts?
faq.answer: You can reduce alerts by working with your building controls contractor to refine alarm thresholds and by filtering out routine events that do not require an immediate physical response.

faq.question: Does Lazur work with my existing facility management software?
faq.answer: Yes, Lazur works with any web-based or desktop application on your Mac. It does not need a direct integration to help you summarize text, point at interface elements, or guide you through your own processes.

costs.title: Operational inefficiency
costs.text: Increased mean time to repair as teams spend time filtering false alarms instead of fixing real issues.

costs.title: Equipment damage
costs.text: Delayed maintenance on critical systems leads to higher long-term repair costs and potential premature hardware failure.

costs.title: Staff burnout
costs.text: Constant, non-stop alerts cause significant stress, which can lead to higher turnover in your maintenance team.

causes.title: Lack of context
causes.text: Systems often notify you of an event without providing data on asset criticality or service history.

causes.title: Fragmented systems
causes.text: Using disconnected tools like spreadsheets and email prevents a unified view of your building health.

causes.title: Data overload
causes.text: Modern building automation systems generate more data than a human can manually process without proper filtering.

fixes.title: Refine alarm thresholds
fixes.text: Work with your controls contractor to disable non-critical alerts that do not require an immediate site visit.

fixes.title: Apply risk-based scoring
fixes.text: Move from static alerts to a system that considers asset age and criticality when ranking notifications.

fixes.title: Centralize communication
fixes.text: Use email rules in your Mac apps to separate routine notifications from urgent maintenance requests.
